data.title: Huckabee points to 3 factors in many Americans turning against Israel
data.description:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee laid out multiple reasons why Americans may be turning against Israel in an interview Thursday — the same day Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended the country’s actions at the United Nations General Assembly.

Huckabee pointed to social media disinformation and foreign propaganda, a lack of “biblical literacy” and a hatred toward people who accept that “there is a God and that he’s made up the rules for life” are to blame for Americans’ rising dissatisfaction towards Israel. 

“You add all that together, I guess you just want to be mad at Israel and blame them for everything,” Huckabee said during a discussion with NewsNation’s Leland Vittert.

“And it’s very unfortunate because Israel has actually given to the world and especially to America and our partnership some very valuable things,” he added.

According to Pew Research Center survey, favorable views of the Israeli government have dropped in recent years, with 62 percent of Americans holding an unfavorable view of nation’s government. A wide partisan gap has appeared as well, with 51 percent of Republicans holding favorable opinions of the Netanyahu-led government while only 16 percent of Democrats feel the same. Americans also have low confidence in Netanyahu himself.

While Democrats have more widely criticized Israel in recent years, Republicans have also changed their tone on the Middle Eastern ally, particularly since the start of the Iran war early this year, which was launched in tandem with Israel.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) called Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide, while conservative commentator Tucker Carlson has been critical of both the Gaza war and Israel’s role in pushing the U.S. into Iran. Carlson travelled to Israel for a tense interview with Huckabee in February.

They Greene and Carlson are both part of a small but loud segment of Trump’s MAGA coalition that says the president has broken his promise to stay out of foreign wars and put “America first.”

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., disputed the falling statistics in an interview this week, blaming the way the questions were asked for the low scores. Danon told The Hill that he believes the majority of Americans “appreciate the bond and alliance between the people” of the U.S. and Israel.

Huckabee has been criticized by figures including Rep. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) for claiming Israel has a biblical claim to land beyond its current borders, and that it would “be fine” if Israel expanded across the region along with actions.

“He’s become a complete apologist for the most extreme Israeli government in history,” Van Hollen said. “He should be defending Americans and defending American interests, he’s failed to do so.”

Huckabee argued claims that Israeli actions in Gaza were genocidal or that it is an apartheid state are wrong and that people will have to be willing to “look at truth” to start to improve American views of the nation.

“This is a place where Muslims, Druze, Christians serve in the military. They vote. They can be in the Knesset. Quite a few Arabs are in the Knesset,” Huckabee said. “They serve on the Supreme Court. They run some of the biggest businesses in the country. If you’re apartheid, that’s not making any sense.”

“I think it’s somewhat of a spiritual problem where people just don’t want to hear the truth because they want to be mad at somebody,” Huckabee said. “Well, let’s pick on the Jews.”

data.title: Senate approves legislation targeted at pilot, air traffic control mental health guidance
data.description:
The Senate passed two bills Thursday aimed at removing barriers for pilots and air traffic controllers seeking mental health treatment, as well as reduce stigma surrounding these conditions.

Sponsored by Sens. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), respectively, both pieces of legislation passed in the upper chamber by unanimous consent. 

The first act, which Hoeven introduced, would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers struggling with mental health issues to seek treatment. It would also provide “enhanced” training for aviation medical examiners on how to address these conditions. 

The bill honors John A. Hauser, an aviation student from Chicago who took his own life in 2021 while attending the University of North Dakota.

“Our nation faces a severe shortage of qualified pilots and air traffic controllers, while bureaucratic delays and outdated processes at the FAA keep these professionals from working for prolonged periods when they seek mental health care,” Hoeven said in a statement after senators passed the package.

The other bill, brought forth by Duckworth, seeks to boost transparency around available medications for aviation industry employees.

This legislation, titled the “Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2026,” would direct the FAA to create and annually update a list of medications that can be safely prescribed to pilots and air traffic controllers. 

“Our aviation system depends on the well-being of our pilots and air traffic controllers, who operate under an immense amount of stress,” Duckworth said in a statement. “Their careers should never be threatened because they weren’t properly informed about which medications they’re allowed to take, or simply sought the mental health care they need.”  

Both bills now head to the House for consideration. 

Earlier this year, the FAA issued new guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers to seek counseling, as well as other mental health services. The Hill has reached out to the agency for comment on the Senate’s approval of these two bills.

data.title: Jack Smith to testify before Senate Judiciary next week
data.description:
Former special counsel Jack Smith will testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday, his second appearance before Congress as they probe his investigation into President Trump.

Smith led a team of Justice Department investigators and ultimately determined he would bring charges against Trump in both the Mar-a-Lago documents case and another related to the president’s actions on Jan. 6, 2021.

Smith will be sitting across from the Judiciary chairman, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), one of Congress’s most vocal critical of the prosecutor’s work.

Grassley’s team has titled the hearing “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans.”

He has repeatedly released documents he has obtained about Smith’s investigation, including toll records showing that Smith reviewed call logs of some senators who spoke with Trump on Jan. 6. Smith did not have access to the content of the calls.

Democrats framed the hearing as a chance for Smith to defend a well-founded investigation.

“Donald Trump spent months spreading the Big Lie and pressuring election officials & Members of Congress to help overturn the 2020 election. Jack Smith investigated this criminal effort.

Finally on Tuesday, Mr. Smith will be able to tell the Senate Judiciary Committee his story,” Senate Judiciary Democrats wrote on their account on X.

Smith testified before the House Judiciary Committee in January.

In closed door testimony in December, Smith defended bringing the cases.

“If asked whether to prosecute a former president based on the same facts today, I would do so regardless of whether the president was a Republican or Democrat,” Smith said in his prepared remarks. 

“The decision to bring charges against President Trump was mine, but the basis for those charges rests entirely with President Trump and his actions, as alleged in the indictments returned by grand juries in two different districts,” the former special counsel added.

data.title: Trump rules out Bessent as AI czar
data.description:
President Trump said on Friday he is ruling out Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to serve as his artificial intelligence czar amid speculation the Cabinet member was under consideration.

Trump, in a Truth Social post Friday, said Bessent will not be the “Super Intelligence (SI) Czar,” referring to his proposed rebrand of AI, because he “doesn’t want to.

“Number Two, he’s doing such a great job at Treasury, and that’s where I want to keep him!” the president continued. “Why would I ever make such a change? Just more Fake News!”

Multiple media reports this week suggested Bessent’s name was being floated for the role, which Trump said he was creating last week to oversee the technology’s development.

The role, which Trump called “AI czar” until saying the government should refer to the technology as “Super Intelligence” or “SI” earlier this week, is likely to help lead a new “AI Force.” The president compared the proposed body to the Space Force, which he established during his first term, but did not disclose how the agency would work.

Bessent became one of the Trump administration’s loudest voices on AI this year, threading the needle for support of U.S. competitiveness in the space and the need for guardrails amid emerging cybersecurity risks.

In the wake of Anthropic’s Mythos model release last spring, Bessent argued the administration’s pro-industry approach is not mutually exclusive with safety. The openness to safety protocols differs slightly from the commander-in-chief, who has largely dismissed concerns around AI and the need for regulations.

The Treasury chief has also had a role in navigating the U.S.’s talks with China over AI.

Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s meeting with Trump this week, he spoke publicly on the U.S.’s proposal for a notification system between Washington and Beijing as concerns mount over the technology’s risks to humanity.

Bessent took an aggressive stance against China in July after the U.S. found Chinese AI companies could be stealing proprietary information from U.S. private models and threatened sanctions over the allegations.

Venture capitalist David Sacks previously held the role of Trump’s AI and crypto czar, but departed the White House earlier this year after his special government employee term expired. Sacks is still a prominent voice in Trump’s ear and co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), which advises the president on policy.

It is not clear who Trump is seriously considering for the role at this time.

Announcing the role last week, the president said, “Only High I.Q. individuals need to apply!” and did not detail how this could differ from Sacks’ position.

data.title: Trump confirms he will meet with Xi two more times this year
data.description:
President Trump on Friday confirmed he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping two more times before the end of the year, following his counterpart’s three-day state visit to the U.S. 

Trump said in a Truth Social post that he will meet with Xi in China in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting, as well as in December during the Group of 20 Summit in Miami. 

“President Xi and Madam Peng have just left D.C., heading for China. The meeting was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the U.S.A.,” Trump wrote. “Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!” 

Earlier Friday, during a tea with Trump and first lady Melania Trump, Xi said he and Trump will have two more opportunities to meet this year in China and the U.S. 

“We will,” Trump said, responding to Xi’s initial invitation. 

Xi wrapped his second state visit to the U.S. on Friday. He last visited the country during former President Obama’s administration in 2015. 

Trump literally rolled out the red carpet for Xi despite facing criticism on both sides of the aisle over the historically adversarial relationship between Washington and Beijing.

Republican and Democratic senators cited allegations that China has aided Iran in its war against the U.S., as well as Beijing’s poor human rights record.

Trump himself criticized Obama for his lavish welcome of Xi at the time.  

Trump told reporters Friday he and Xi discussed the Iran war. U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue also said Trump made it clear to Xi that China helping Iran is unacceptable. 

The two leaders also discussed artificial intelligence during their meetings. The U.S. president also suggested there could be an agriculture deal in the works. 

“I think our farmers are going to be very happy, a lot of very positive things happened,” Trump said.

data.title: Trump criticized Obama's state dinner for Xi before holding his own
data.description:
President Trump criticized former President Barack Obama for hosting Chinese presidents for state dinners, including Xi Jinping, multiple times over a decade before doing it himself.

Trump personally greeted Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday and hosted a state dinner for him on Thursday.

But back in 2016, Trump criticized state dinners, saying, “we shouldn’t have dinners at all.”

“We should be eating a hamburger on a conference table, and we should make better deals with China and others and forget the state dinners,” he said at a rally, adding that they “cost a fortune.”

In 2015, he said on Fox News that he wouldn’t be throwing Xi a state dinner.

“I would not be throwing him a dinner…I’d get him a McDonald’s hamburger and I’d say, ‘We gotta get down to work,’” he said at the time. “You know, we’ll give him a state dinner and what he’s done is sucked all of our jobs and he’s sucked the money right out of our country.”

He slammed Obama in 2012 for hosting then-Vice President Xi, including his visit to the Pentagon where he received military honors.

“So wrong! @BarackObama is hosting China’s VP Xi Jinping today at the Pentagon with a full honor ceremony with music and cannons…” he wrote.

He also criticized Obama in 2011 for hosting then-Chinese President Hu Jintao for a state dinner.

“We have the president of China come a few months ago to Washington and we give him a state dinner,” he said at the time. “Now, when people are screwing you, you don’t give them state dinners.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on the tarmac of JBA. They were greeted by military bands, two children bearing bouquets, a canon salute and a flyover of two B1 bombers.

Xi was in the U.S. for a three-day state visit. But his visit received criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

“I know the President intends to discuss trade and AI with the Chinese leadership — and rightfully so… But, during every minute of dialogue, our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America,” Sen Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said on the Senate floor Tuesday night.

A group of Democratic senators released a statement slamming Trump’s invite to Xi.

“As Americans face rising prices for gas, food, housing, and more, President Trump is rolling out the red carpet for President Xi and hosting closed-door dinners so his billionaire friends can strike deals that threaten American jobs and national security,” they wrote.

When Trump traveled to Beijing earlier this year, he also got a red carpet at the airport but was greeted by China’s Vice President Han Zheng instead.

Trump praised Xi’s visit Friday, saying “tremendous strides” have been made for both countries.

“A lot of very positive things happened, but America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” he continued. “Great things for both countries, and it’s been just very, very productive.”

data.title: Lesbian bars are dwindling across the US. How online outrage over mask policy dispute thrust one into the spotlight
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Lesbian bars have been disappearing across the country for decades.

With only 36 lesbian bars left in the entire country, according to the Lesbian Bar Project, one of the last ones standing getting caught in a fight over its own mask policy raises a bigger question: Why fight over rules for a bar that might not be around much longer anyway?

That’s the argument Jane Velez-Mitchell, founder and host of the nonprofit streaming network UnchainedTV, made on NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight,” discussing backlash against Last Ditch in Greenfield, Mass., after its owner proposed easing a mask mandate in place since 2020.

The number of lesbian bars across the U.S. has been shrinking since the 1980s, when they numbered around 200, according to Newsweek.

“We deal with misogyny and violence and threats that make us want to maintain some exclusivity with who is welcomed into the spaces,” the former general manager of New York City’s Cubbyhole told the outlet. “It’s really important that lesbian bars hold space for everyone’s gender journey.”

Amid changing dietary habits and the rise of app-based dating, some say bars just aren’t an attractive venue anymore.

“We don’t need to go to bars to meet people anymore,” Velez-Mitchell said. “That’s why lesbian bars are closing.” She pointed to online dating and said some patrons are also drinking less, describing herself as a “sober lesbian vegan” who doesn’t rely on bars to socialize.

Beck & Stone senior consultant Emma Jo Morris acknowledged some business logic in catering to existing customers, saying “you don’t tell your client what your client wants… your job is to serve the client.”

Host Katie Pavlich pushed back, saying she believed “the general public is over” masks and said keeping the rule could cost the bar new business.

After making national headlines, the bar has been flooded with critical online “reviews” from people thousands of miles away.

Velez-Mitchell said the shrinking market predates this controversy, however. Last Ditch got its name, she said, because two other gay bars in the area had already closed. She tied the decline to changing times rather than any single policy, pointing to how routine public visibility has become for gay couples.

“I just walked for an hour with two friends of mine, a lesbian couple. They were holding hands the whole way and nobody blinked,” she said, adding that the same walk would have drawn stares 22 years ago.

data.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror ready to return to normal: Reports
data.description:
(NewsNation) — The holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy case is ready to get back to normal after a surge of publicity following the trial.

Michael Desronvil said he is planning to return to his day job next week, with his attorney Edward Patlzik telling TMZ that his client had been laying low since the end of the trial.

The trial for Lindsay Clancy, accused of killing her three young children, lasted more than five weeks, followed by seven days of jury deliberations. The case ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach an agreement.

Desronvil needed time to process what happened, Paltzik said, spending time with his girlfriend and attending church.

He made headlines after being revealed as the lone juror voting to find Clancy guilty.

Prosecutors argued that Clancy had committed a premeditated crime when killing her children, while the defense argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and not criminally responsible for her actions.

The jury of nine women and three men was split, with 11 jurors voting to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

Following the trial, the jury foreperson and other jurors came forward with criticisms of Desronvil, suggesting that he was ignoring the judge’s instructions on reasonable doubt.

He denied those allegations, saying he believes Clancy is guilty of the crime.

Since the trial, he said he had been doxxed and had his personal and legal history made public by people online who disagreed with his position.

Defense Attorney Kevin Reddington has called for an investigation into Desronvil to examine his conduct during the trial, his answers on a pretrial questionnaire and allegations that he used his cell phone during deliberations.

Paltzik pushed back against that motion, saying that investigating jury members would have a chilling effect on people’s willingness to serve on a jury and start a cycle where lawyers investigate any jury when they disagree with the results.

data.title: 'Give Like Dolly Day' brings Imagination Library donations from companies
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Friday is “Give Like Dolly Day,” a day dedicated to supporting the late Dolly Parton’s philanthropic legacy, the Imagination Library, a program geared toward helping children learn to read by providing access to free books.

Give Like Dolly Day was announced Sept. 14 and set to take place Sept. 25, mirroring Dolly’s hit song “9 to 5.”

“Give Like Dolly Day will shine a light on Imagination Library Partners and encourage communities to rally around them and other local organizations helping children where they live,” the Dollywood Foundation said in the announcement.

The Imagination Library was inspired by Parton’s father, who could not read or write. Since its founding in 1995, the foundation has grown to serve children across the United States, as well as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia and Canada.

Here are some organizations donating proceeds to the Imagination Library.

1. American Eagle

American Eagle announced all proceeds from two items, the Dolly Jean and the Dolly Parton Graphic Tee, will be donated to the Imagination Library.

The Dolly Jean was formerly the AE Super-High Waisted Flare Jean. This item is available in both stores and online, the tee is available exclusively online.

2. Regal Cinema

Regal Cinema will be screening “Steel Magnolias” and “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas” in Parton’s memory Friday, with tickets priced at $9.25.

“All proceeds will go to Dolly’s childhood literacy foundation, the Imagination Library through the Regal Foundation,” Regal posted in a promotional statement.

3. Hatti B’s Hot Chicken

In a post on Facebook, the company announced it will be donating all orders placed at one of its Tennessee locations to the Imagination Library.

“Must be a qualifying order that includes an entree,” the post reads. “Value of one book donated per order. Must order directly from Hattie Bs in restaurant, web, or app.”

4. Jenni’s Ice Cream

The ice cream company will be donating 25 percent of sales from two Dolly-inspired flavors to the Imagination Library, according to a post on Instagram.

The flavors are called “Dough-lene” and “Scoop of Ambition.” The orders must be placed from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. at any location.

5. The Protein Bar

The Protein Bar will be offering a limited-edition shake, The Dolly, and donating 25 percent of sales from locations in Chicago and downtown Indianapolis to the Imagination Library.

“A shake that sparkles inside and out, just like Dolly herself,” the company said in an Instagram post.

data.title: Collins warns OMB about unspent global health funding
data.description:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, is calling on the Trump administration to spend more than $1 billion of global health funding that Congress has already appropriated before it expires Sept. 30. 

In a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Budget Director Russ Vought and Eric Ueland — the Trump aide in charge of the remnants of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) — Collins warned that $1.3 billion appropriated in fiscal year 2025 must be spent as intended. 

The Maine Republican said she doesn’t want to see the funding expire, or for the administration use the money for “unknown closeout costs” related to the decision to shutter USAID.  

“I urge USAID to ensure that the funding is spent to combat public health threats consistent with congressional intent, either by obligating the funding prior to the end of the fiscal year or transferring funds to the Department for such purposes,” she wrote.  

The funding was meant to protect maternal and child health and counter infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. 

The letter comes on the heels of a warning earlier this week from top Senate Democrats about the administration’s decision to redirect more than $2 billion in appropriated foreign aid funding to closing down the agency.

Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) — the Senate’s top Democratic appropriator and the top Democrat on the panel that funds the State Department— said the administration is diverting the $1.3 billion for global health programs, as well as $1.2 billion for development assistance. 

They added that the Trump administration plans to let an additional $725 million expire Sept. 30 instead of spending it.  

That figure includes $115 million to combat the international illicit narcotics trade, human trafficking, and other international crimes; $310 million to counter Russia with U.S. assistance in Europe and Eurasia; and $300 million and invest in secure supply chains and American competitiveness through economic growth programs. 

“Congress passed a law to invest in saving lives … it did not hand Trump a checkbook to spend on whatever he pleases while blocking funding for everything else,” Schatz and Murray said in a joint statement.

“The Trump administration needs to rework its plans and spend these resources as Congress intended, and we need Republicans in Congress to finally join us in insisting that happens,” the senators added. 

OMB did not immediately respond to questions about what it plans to do with the money.
